newsitem.title: USA: Factory orders weaken as economy slows.
newsitem.headline: Factory orders weaken as economy slows.

text.p: New orders to U.S. factories tumbled at the sharpest rate in 3-1/2 years during August, the Commerce Department said Thursday, as the economy's industrial sector lost some of its vigour.

Orders were down a surprisingly steep 1.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted $311.1 billion -- the largest monthly decline since a 2.2 percent decrease in January 1993. Backlogs of unfilled orders weakened and inventories mounted.
The August decline more than erased a 1.7 percent July orders gain.

Separately, the Labour Department reported new applications for jobless pay were steady last week at 340,000, the same as in the prior week, though a four-week moving average picked up for a seventh straight week.
"Both of these numbers support the view that the economy will be moderating for the balance of the year," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla.

A second-quarter "boomlet" during which the economy surged at a two-year peak rate of 4.7 percent was giving way to slower growth around 2.5 percent in the third quarter and 3 percent in the fourth quarter, she predicted.

That remains above the economy's long-term potential growth rate of 2 percent to 2-1/4 percent a year that is considered safely non-inflationary, so Federal Reserve policymakers likely will remain on edge.

"The Fed faces an unfriendly environment in which wage pressures are going to keep building even as the economy moderates," Reaser noted, especially if there is a modest rebound in growth in the closing quarter as expected.
Last week, a four-week moving average of jobless claims rose to 334,500 from 328,750 the week before, the highest reading since an average of 312,500 claims for the week ended June 10, 1996.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, asked about the factory orders falloff, said there was no cause for worry about the economy if a six- to 12-month view was considered.
"I think far and away the most likely scenario is continuation of solid growth, obviously not at the same level as the second quarter," he said.

The August falloff in factory orders followed a revised 1.7 percent July increase that was previously reported as a stronger 1.8 percent gain. Orders have fallen in two of the past three months including a 0.7 percent June decrease.
Demand faded for both expensive durable goods like cars and airplanes and for more quickly used nondurables like food and paper products.
Durables orders dropped a revised 3.2 percent to $166.8 billion in August after a 1.4 percent July rise, while nondurables orders were down 0.4 percent following a 1.9 percent jump in July.
Previously, the department said durables orders had fallen 3.1 percent in August but it revised that fractionally.

"For the most part, these are relatively soft numbers which are more in line with an economy that is growing at a moderate, sustainable pace," said Joel Naroff, a Philadelphia-based economist for First Union Corp. of Charlotte, N.C.

Naroff said a 0.3 percent fall in August order backogs and a second straight monthly rise in stocks of unsold goods "imply that manufacturers are not being overburdened by too much demand and will therefore not be pressed to raise prices" to the Fed's relief.
The biggest factor in the durables orders decline was transportation equipment as orders plunged 7.9 percent to $37.9 billion after declines of 1.5 percent in July and 1.3 percent in June.
The department said aircraft and parts were the major cause for the transportation slump in August, although new-car orders also were down from July.
Excluding transportation, August factory orders still were down 1.1 percent, the largest decline since a 1.5 percent drop in May 1993, after a 2.1 percent rise in July.
Weaker factory orders were anticipated in view of other recent signs of continued cooling in manufacturing activity.
On Tuesday, the National Association of Manufacturers said its September index of activity dipped to 51.7 from 52.6 in August as production, employment and export orders slowed.
Shipments of manufactured goods, reflecting more immediate demand than orders, were up in August by a slight 0.1 percent to $312.6 billion after a strong 1.1 percent July rise.
Only defence orders posted an August increase, up 10 percent to $5.3 billion after a 40.7 percent drop in July.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, dropped 10.2 percent to $41.3 billion after a 7 percent rise in July.
